A DATA STORY · HACKER STATISTICS

What are the chances of winning the bet?

A dice-climbing bet, simulated thousands of times, then checked with exact math, statistics and machine learning.

Scott Schirkofsky · schirko.com/scott/hacker-statistics

The bet: roll a die 100 times and climb to step 60

1 or 2

Step down one. You can never fall below step 0.

3, 4 or 5

Step up one.

6

Roll again and climb that many steps.

Clumsy

Every roll there is a 0.1% chance of falling back to step 0.

One climb is just one story

  • The line is one climb of 100 rolls. This one finished on step 80.
  • Each step depends on the one before, so this is a random walk.
  • One story can't tell us the odds. So we repeat it.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky3 / 13

Climb 10,000 times and the odds appear

  • Each line is one simulated climb.
  • Blue climbs reached step 60. Grey ones did not.
  • The sharp drops to zero are the clumsy falls.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky4 / 13

About 78 in 100 climbs reach step 60

  • 77.5% of 10,000 simulated climbs finished at or above 60.
  • 95% interval: 76.7% to 78.4%.
  • The average climb ends near step 72.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky5 / 13

Clumsiness costs about 6 points

  • Without falls: 83.7%.
  • With the 0.1% fall chance: 77.7%.
  • Over 100 rolls, 9.5% of climbs take at least one fall to zero.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky6 / 13

The exact math agrees with the simulation

  • The game is a Markov chain: each roll only depends on where you stand.
  • Tracking every step's probability gives the exact answer: 77.7%.
  • The simulated bars follow the exact line.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky7 / 13

How many walks are enough?

  • The estimate settles as walks are added; the band is its 95% interval.
  • Error shrinks with the square root of the walks: 4x the walks, half the error.
  • A bootstrap and a Bayesian posterior tell the same story.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky8 / 13

You can know your odds mid-game

  • At the start: 77.7%.
  • After roll 30 on step 40: 93%. On step 20: 77%.
  • Calculated backwards from the last roll, this is a value function, an idea from reinforcement learning.
  • The pale band is the line of no return.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky9 / 13

Machine learning learns the same odds

  • A logistic regression and a small neural network, trained on 4,000 climbs and tested on 1,000 new ones.
  • Accuracy 78.2% for both, against 76.6% for always guessing the base rate.
  • Log loss 0.491 for both, against 0.489 for the exact answer.
  • They drift a little high at the far right, where few climbs exist. No model can beat the exact curve.
Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky10 / 13

More ways to look at the same climbs

Clustering

k-means groups climbs by shape. The groups line up with who won, though the outcome was never used.

Outlier detection

Robust z-scores flag the unusual walks. Most are unlucky climbs that fell late.

Autocorrelation

Roll-to-roll changes are unpredictable, so it is a true random walk, with a drift near three-quarters of a step per roll.

Hypothesis tests

A chi-square test says the die is fair. A z-test says clumsiness really does lower the odds.

Hacker Statistics · Scott Schirkofsky11 / 13

Why this matters beyond the dice

Money and risk

Simulate thousands of market paths to see the chance a portfolio runs out, or how bad a bad year could get. Insurers ask how often big claims pile up.

Planning and supply chains

Simulate delays and demand to find the chance a project finishes on time, or how much stock to hold so shelves are not empty.

Science and medicine

Estimate how often a study of a given size would find a real effect, or how a disease might spread.

When to act

The roll-or-stop game turns "what are my odds?" into "when should I stop?", the same question as in trading, pricing and cutting a project's losses. A learning program can find the best rule from practice alone (notebook 06).

A good bet

About 78 times in 100. The exact answer is 77.7%.

The risk

A fall back to zero. The 0.1% fall chance costs about 6 points.

Every method agrees

Simulation, exact math and machine learning all give the same answer.
